one_liner: x86-64 CRC-32C in one function: three interleaved SSE4.2 crc32 streams recombined with PCLMULQDQ, ~2.9x a single-stream crc32 loop.
what_it_does: It computes CRC-32C (Castagnoli, the polynomial built into the x86 crc32 instruction) over a buffer of any length and alignment, via uint32_t option_13_golden_intel(const void* M, uint32_t bytes, uint32_t prev = 0), plus a 2-way variant option_14_golden_amd tuned for AMD Jaguar (PS4/Xbox One). The repo is really a long README tutorial plus a Visual Studio benchmark that derives 13 CRC methods, from bitwise MASM loops through slicing-by-1..16 tables to hardware crc32, and times them against each other. The reusable part is the self-contained golden_intel.cpp (or golden_amd.cpp): one function plus a precomputed shift-constant LUT.
how_it_is_fast: A single _mm_crc32_u64 chain is latency-bound (3-cycle latency, 1-per-cycle throughput on Intel), which caps it at about 21.3 bits/cycle. Golden splits each block of up to 6 KiB into three equal parts and runs three independent crc32 chains in parallel. It then merges them by carry-less multiplying (PCLMULQDQ) the A and B partial CRCs with precomputed constants CRC(x^k) from a 256-entry LUT, and folds the result into C's last 8-byte word with one more crc32. Block sizes are dispatched through a fully unrolled 255-case switch generated by 'doubler' macros (765 crc32 instructions), and a multiply-shift (x*2731>>16) replaces division by 24. The technique matches Intel's 2011 'Fast CRC Computation for iSCSI Polynomial Using CRC32 Instruction' whitepaper, and the README derives it from first principles.
when_to_use: x86-64 code that must checksum KB-to-MB buffers with CRC-32C (the iSCSI/ext4/Btrfs polynomial) and is limited by a plain _mm_crc32_u64 loop. Here Golden measured 62 vs 21.3 bits/cycle, and an HN user reported ~32 GB/s on an i7-4770K.
You want a small MIT-licensed function to vendor (one .cpp, a 2 KB LUT, no dependencies) rather than a library with a build system.

Game-engine style integrity checks (save data, cooked assets, memory-stomp detection), which are the author's stated use case. Use the 2-way option_14_golden_amd on AMD Jaguar consoles, where crc32 reciprocal throughput is 2 cycles.
Learning or teaching CRC optimization: the README walks from bitwise CRC through slicing-by-N to the parallel crc32 + CLMUL recombine, and HN commenters cite it as the standard overview.
when_not_to_use: You need IEEE CRC-32 (zlib, gzip, PNG, ZIP, Ethernet). The x86 crc32 instruction hard-codes the Castagnoli polynomial, and the author confirms in issue #2 that Golden cannot be changed to match zlib. Use a PCLMULQDQ-folding implementation such as crc32fast, klauspost/crc32 or crc-fast instead.

You want the fastest CRC-32C on current x86. corsix's 'fusion' of crc32 and pclmulqdq streams measured ~93 bits/cycle against ~54-57 for this three-way design on Broadwell/Skylake/Ice Lake, and corsix/fast-crc32 AVX-512 kernels reach 97.30 GB/s on Sapphire Rapids.

Short messages. Below LEAF_SIZE (144 bytes on Intel, 112 on AMD) it only runs the plain 8-byte crc32 loop, so there is no gain over the single-stream baseline, and there is also a byte-wise alignment prologue.

Non-x86 targets, or binaries that must run on CPUs without SSE4.2 and PCLMULQDQ. There is no runtime dispatch or portable fallback in the Golden files, and the tabular options are demo code (see gotchas). On ARM, see dougallj's M1 gist or corsix/fast-crc32.

You need a maintained, tested library. The only build is a Windows VS2019 solution, there are no unit tests (main.cpp just prints each option's CRC for visual comparison), and the last commit was in April 2021.

integration.form: source-drop (copy golden_intel.cpp or golden_amd.cpp; the repo itself is a Visual Studio benchmark solution, not a library)
integration.min_toolchain: The repo builds with Visual Studio 2019 (v142 toolset) for x64; options 1-4 need MASM. Golden itself is C++11-level code (constexpr, a default argument). The README discusses GCC and other compilers' codegen, but only MSVC project files ship; with GCC or Clang you would need -msse4.2 -mpclmul or equivalent (inferred, not tested).
integration.platforms: x86-64 only, with SSE4.2 (crc32) and PCLMULQDQ. It uses _mm_crc32_u64 and pointer-to-uint64_t casts, so the solution's Win32 configurations cannot build it. The Intel variant is tuned for crc32 at 3-cycle latency and 1/cycle throughput, the AMD variant for Jaguar's 1 per 2 cycles.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. The Golden functions only read a static const LUT and write no globals, so concurrent calls look safe from the source.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the (buffer, length, prev) -> uint32_t shape fits a CRC-32C routine, but by default it skips the standard ~init/~final inversion, so outputs differ from iSCSI CRC-32C until two commented lines are enabled. It can never replace zlib's IEEE crc32().

gotchas: The shipped code does not produce standard CRC-32C. golden_intel.cpp and golden_amd.cpp start from prev and return the raw register with the ~ lines commented out, while the README's listing inverts both. Issue #2 shows 'hello-world' giving 1585878819 here against 4099351003 from htot/crc32c; the author's answer was to uncomment those two lines.

The tabular 'portable' options are demos. Options 9 and 10 loop while (bytes) { ...; bytes -= 8 or 16; } on a uint32_t, so any length that is not a multiple of 8 or 16 wraps around and reads far past the buffer; the issue #2 reporter hit a segfault going down this path. They also read native-endian 32-bit words and apply no init or final XOR.

There is no CPU feature check: calling Golden on a CPU without SSE4.2/PCLMULQDQ faults with an illegal instruction. The provided Release x64 project compiles everything with /arch:AVX2, so rebuild with a lower /arch before targeting AVX-only CPUs such as Jaguar, which option 14 exists for.

The length is a uint32_t, so each call handles under 4 GiB; chain larger buffers through prev. Loads are type-punned (*(uint64_t*)p), and for n == 256 the _mm_loadu_si128 of g_lut_intel[n-1] nominally reads 8 bytes past the 256-entry LUT, although only the low 8 bytes are used.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it when you want the most readable, easily vendored x86-64 CRC-32C (one MIT-licensed function) together with the best-known derivation of the three-way crc32 + CLMUL technique. For more throughput use corsix/fast-crc32. For IEEE CRC-32 or ARM use crc32fast, crc-fast or klauspost/crc32. htot/crc32c wraps Intel's original crc_iscsi_v_pcl assembly for the same algorithm, adds a 32-bit port and is BSD-2-licensed.
verified_claims_summary: The README table comes from CRC/main.cpp, which times each method on the same 900 KiB mt19937 buffer for 20-10000 runs and converts wall-clock ns to 'bits/cycle' by assuming a 4 GHz clock. The CPU is described only as a 'high-end modern x86 CPU', and the compiler is unstated; the repo's project is MSVC v142 /O2 /arch:AVX2. Golden's 62 bits/cycle (about 31 GB/s under the 4 GHz assumption) compares with 21.3 for a single-stream 8-byte crc32 loop (~2.9x) and 8.0 for slicing-by-16 (~7.75x), all of them the author's own implementations rather than zlib or a named library. Independently, corsix measured the same three-way structure at 53.7-56.5 bits/cycle (27-33 GB/s) on 4 KiB buffers across Broadwell, Skylake and Ice Lake, and 23.5 GB/s on AMD Rome.
status_note: Abandoned since 2021-04-25 (the last commits were typo and comment fixes, and the one open issue is corsix's 2022 'alloy' note), but MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor: copy golden_intel.cpp, decide on the ~init/~final lines, and compile with SSE4.2 and PCLMUL enabled.
